# Public Data APIs: Our Water Main {#sec-noaa-api} 

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

source("R/_common.R")
```

Hey analyst! Welcome to **🌧️ Raining Tables Chapter 2** 🌧️ 

Hold onto your hats! 🪁 Today, we're hooking up to our NOAA API water main. No more hauling csvs around; we'll have our data on tap. 🚰 

Said differently: instead of manually re-downloading a csv every update, our scripts will call NOAA's API directly and pull their data into our programming environment.

✨ ~ *pretty amazing* ~ ✨

So how do APIs work?

:::{.callout-note}
## What's an API?

An API, or [Application Programming Interface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/API), is an application programming interface to connect computers or pieces of software. In contrast to a user interface, APIs run "under the hood" and aren't intended to be used directly by people other than the programmer incorporating it into software.[^1] As programmers, if we're using an API, we're "calling" the API, in our case to request data directly from NOAA's CDO database, and NOAA is the institution "hosting" the API. 

For our purposes, updating an analysis automatically, the NOAA API gives us a way to request data using a script rather than having to manually click through their website's user interface. They've written out [API documentation](https://www.ncdc.noaa.gov/cdo-web/webservices/v2) so we can format our call to retrieve the data we need. Our API call returns this data in an efficient, standardized, and predictable way. 🚰

:::

First, we need to request an `API key`🔑 , a user password we add to our API call so NOAA recognizes us:  

1. Go to NOAA's [API page](https://www.ncdc.noaa.gov/cdo-web/token) to request a key.  
2. Submit the email address you want associated with this project.  
3. They'll send you an email with your `API key` 🔑, a long string of letters and numbers. Copy this string.  
4. Save this string in .Renviron, your [R environment file](https://docs.posit.co/ide/user/ide/guide/environments/r/managing-r.html#renviron) ([example here](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=D2yPyEPMTbo)), so your script knows where to look for it. Don't copy-paste it directly in your code! If you copy-paste into your code, you could expose it when sharing code or posting on GitHub. Saving in .Renviron keeps your password a secret. 🤫

Format API keys in your .Renviron file as:  

> `NOAA_CDO_KEY=abcde12345`

where `NOAA_CDO_KEY` is a memorable name you make up for your key and `abcde12345` is the `API key` 🔑 you received from NOAA. No spaces, no quotes.

Have your API key safely saved in .Renviron? Excellent, let's start! 🥳

## API Calls

Many public data API calls are formatted as a URL that combines your unique `API key` 🔑 with a collection of other parameters to identify and request our specific data cut. A public data API URL typically first specifies a particular database or dataset maintained by the institution. It might also specify a date range, series ID, time frequency, unit of measurement, data flags, or other attributes you can use to  your data cut.

Knowing how to format the call requires reading your data source's API user manual and reviewing provided examples. The format's quite fiddly! If we don't string the parameters together in the exact order, the API call won't go through. 

Let's walk through the NOAA call from [`R/pull_daily_rain`](R/pull_daily_rain.R). Remember we're hooking up to our data source water main ⛲: we'll explore the different pipes, then connect the pipes together and test our taps. 🚰 

### Our API key

For calling data in an analysis, we first save our key as the object `api_key` and use nchar() to check it exists without printing it and exposing it:

```{r}
#| label: api-key

# Sys.getenv() is how we call our key from the .Renviron environment file 🔑
api_key <- Sys.getenv("NOAA_CDO_KEY")
nchar(api_key) # returns 32 if it's set, 0 if it isn't
```

### What we're requesting

We may want many cuts of data, so [`R/pull_daily_rain`](R/pull_daily_rain.R) API call should be flexible enough to easily change the data parameters we care about. For this, we set our data parameters as function arguments. We can then retrieve different cuts of data by changing the arguments. 

To show this concretely, let's set the parameters for a data cut for [zipcode 97205](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Portland,+OR+97205/@45.5173805,-122.740049,13z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x54950a1cf1ebc7d1:0xd47124b9bd5b8f22!8m2!3d45.5205043!4d-122.707349!16s%2Fm%2F020r733?entry=ttu&g_ep=EgoyMDI2MDkyMy4wIKXMDSoASAFQAw%3D%3D), the beautiful but rainy city of Portland, Oregon. 🌧️  

```{r}
#| label: walkthrough-params
zipcode <- "97205"
date_start <- "2024-01-01"
date_end <- "2024-12-31"
units <- "standard"
limit <- 1000

location_params <- paste0("&locationid=ZIP:", zipcode) # specifies we're using zipcodes for location
```

Side note: if you look in [`R/pull_daily_rain`](R/pull_daily_rain.R), you'll see it's our choice to use zip codes to specify location in `location_params`. NOAA also gives us the option to specify location using weather station IDs, IDs for the specific sites weather data are collected. Finding weather station IDs takes a bit more digging, though, so we're using zip codes.  

### The URL

Next, we string our URL strings together, like fitting pipes. 🔧

```{r}
#| label: walkthrough-url

# stringing our data cut parameters to NOAA's URL string:

url_string <- paste0(
  "https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/cdo-web/api/v2/data?", # base url string
  "datasetid=GHCND", # the dataset we want
  "&datatypeid=PRCP", # the data type we want (precipitation)
  location_params, # our location params
  "&startdate=", date_start, # start date
  "&enddate=", date_end, # end date
  "&units=", units, # units of measurement
  "&limit=", limit # how many data observations included in the API's response
)
# just keep stringing 🐟
```

#### URL formats

The NOAA API's base URL string typically won't change *unless* NOAA intentionally updates its backend infrastructure. If we're building a product using NOAA's API, we should subscribe to NOAA updates or notifications so they can communicate those kinds of changes to us. Reliable public data flows and user communications are hallmarks of working #publicdatainfrastructure. 

We've added all the parameters we need for our data cut! Last step: including your `API key` 🔑.

:::{.callout-important}
## Where the API key goes

In the case of the NOAA API, we're not adding our `API key` 🔑 directly into our call URL, as Census and some other public data sources do. NOAA wants it in a request *header*, which is a bit different (see code below).

If a different public data API expects `&api_key=...` directly added to `url_string`, remember the full URL string then contains your `API key` 🔑 and becomes a secret: don't print it, don't log it, don't paste it anywhere. 🤫 For other APIs, review their documentation and check their API call examples.
:::

### Calling our data

```{r}
#| label: walkthrough-send
response <- httr::RETRY(
  verb = "GET",
  url = url_string,
  httr::add_headers(token = api_key),
  httr::timeout(10),
  times = 3,
  pause_base = 1,
  pause_cap = 10,
  quiet = TRUE
)

response
```

`RETRY()` is `GET()` with a fail-safe built in:  

- if the first call doesn't go through, or if the connection times out, it waits and tries again instead of failing.  
- `pause_base = 1` and `pause_cap = 10` create this recurring call for us.  

If we need it, the `response` output above also contains information about our call status (ie, if it ran successfully) and any associated messages. If our call fails, we can check error or other messages by viewing its status:

```{r}
#| label: walkthrough-status
httr::status_code(response)
httr::http_status(response)
```

:::{.callout-tip}
## Seeing the HTTP request in action

As an experiment, let's see our call in action by wrapping it in `httr::with_verbose()`:

```{r}
#| eval: false
httr::with_verbose(
  httr::GET(url_string, httr::add_headers(token = "put-a-fake-token-here"))
)
```

The console output shows us step-by-step what we're doing when we send this call: our request, a request timestamp, where the data are hosted, the content size and type, and whether the call ran successfully:  

`->` shows what we sent. 
`<-` shows what's returned.  

Why use a fake token? The verbose output **prints your headers**, including your `API key`🔑. Remember, if you run it with your real key, you'll reveal the key in your console history or log. This is also why "here's my verbose output" is a common way to leak a key. Watch where you put your keys! 🤫
:::

### What's returned

```{r}
#| label: walkthrough-parse
parsed <- httr::content(response, as = "parsed", type = "application/json")

# as we see, our data are returned with values nested in a named list
str(parsed, max.level = 2)
```

Most APIs return data in a format called [JSON](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nDyiIx0BVq0&t=610s) as a list of nested values. There are two top-level pieces: `metadata`, which describes the response, and `results`, our data.

Under `parsed$metadata`, we can review `parsed$metadata$resultset` to ensure we've collected all the data we asked for, rather than hitting NOAA's data `limit`:

```{r}
#| label: walkthrough-metadata
parsed$metadata$resultset
```

:::{.callout-warning}
## `count` vs. `limit`

`count` shows how many observations NOAA returned from our request, but `limit` is its observation cap. If `count` is larger than `limit`, we didn't get all our data, just the first page, with no error to warn us.

NOAA's ceiling is 1000 observations per request, and a year of daily precipitation data for a given zip code can blow past that. The fix is the `offset` parameter: ask again starting at record 1001, then 2001, until you've got `count` of them.
:::

### Unnesting our table

Finally, let's look at our data. Here's first row of observations in our data, stored as a list of five fields: date, datatype, station, attributes, value.

```{r}
#| label: walkthrough-one-result
str(parsed$results[1])
```

In `parsed$results`, we have hundreds of observations stored the same way. They're nested and inconvenient to access like this, though. Let's convert this list to a dataframe.

```{r}
#| label: walkthrough-bind
rain <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(parsed$results, as.data.frame))

# the first five rows in our dataframe in a simple table
gt::gt(head(rain))
```

`lapply(..., as.data.frame)` turns each one-observation list into a one-row data frame, and `bind_rows()` stacks them together. 

### What if your API call fails?

It's pretty common for API calls to fail on the first try, especially if you're requesting a large amount of data or if your connection's spotty. We can usually resolve this by trying multiple times, like in `httr::RETRY()`. If your call's still failing or simply taking a long time, and you're sure it's not a bug, consider breaking up your data request into smaller cuts. For example, if you're having trouble pulling ten years of data, try two calls pulling five years of data. 

If at first you don't succeed, try, try again! 😆 

More importantly, how do we *know* if our call fails? Unless our program flags the fail, it'll continue running, try to parse the error message, and halt and force us to debug. To prevent this from happening, we need to add checks:

```{r}
#| label: walkthrough-bad-key
#| error: true

# us calling an API with a nonexistent key
bad <- httr::GET(url_string, httr::add_headers(token = "definitely-not-a-token"))

httr::status_code(bad)
httr::stop_for_status(bad, task = "pull data from NOAA CDO API")
```

`stop_for_status()` flags any failed calls. Without it, our script sails on 🌊 ⛵ 🏔️, tries to parse an error message as data 💥 🏔️, and stalls out.
